#996. Still England's best? Bronze and Earps' performances analysed

Digital journalist Laura Hunter returns for a second season with a WSL-dedicated column, analysing all the big talking points from across the weekend's action; this week's focus is on the heroic performances of two England legends Lucy Bronze and Mary Earps

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sky Sports columnist Laura Hunter analyses the big talking points from the sixth round of Women's Super League matches, bringing you closer to the key stories at the heart of the women's game.

Nothing makes Lucy Bronze prouder than a clean sheet. She absolutely thrives off the scrap and skirmish of it. Against Manchester City, her determination to put defensive duty above all else won Chelsea a priceless three points.

Not since November 2025 had the WSL's leading scorer Khadija Shaw failed to register a shot on target in a game. Bronze can pocket that achievement. She had help from other members of the backline - Veerle Buurman was standout too - but Chelsea's captain led the lockdown.

Shaw was isolated, limited in time and space, and restricted in her movement. "We had to be like dogs in this game," Bronze told BBC Sport afterwards. "We were very focused on that." They shackled Shaw in a way few defences across Europe are able to, Bronze acting as the technical and tactical lynchpin.

This, Chelsea's biggest win of the season so far, is one that sees them leapfrog their greatest rivals in the race for this year's title. It will be a campaign built on solidity as much as anything else. The Blues have given up a miserly 0.5 goals per 90 so far.

Sonia Bompastor had stressed the importance of winning duels pre-game and that emphasis ran through the spine of her team. She made a point of praising Bronze's leadership in the handling of City's threats post-match, capping a heroic display with a game-high 13 defensive contributions.

Collectively, Chelsea won the duel count 47-37 and were equally better in possession, with more systematic and sustained pressure in the opposition half. Bronze won that contest too. No Chelsea player created more chances (2) or completed more final third passes (9) than her. She also registered more touches than any team-mate (87).

Meanwhile, Shaw was reduced to taking 45 per cent of her open play touches in City's defensive half and received more passes from goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita (6) than any outfield player. City's usual rhythm was heavily disrupted and meant the striker blanked in a league game for the first time this season.

Even in the second half, when Andree Jeglertz adjusted his setup to bring Vivianne Miedema into the pocket behind Shaw, Chelsea adapted to match up. Bronze smelt the danger, commanding others to follow her exemplary lead.

A situation in the 75th minute summed up Chelsea's application perfectly.

The ball is punched through the lines to Shaw, usually so reliable in her hold-up play. But on this occasion Buurman is encouraged to engage aggressively and the ball turns over. Aggie Beever-Jones and Maika Hamano exchange passes on halfway, before the latter opts to go long in search of Alyssa Thompson's far side run.

The sequence of events that follow spell the beginning of the end for City. Yamashita feels compelled to try and cut out the pass but is caught in no man's land, mistiming her intervention and gets sent off for denying Thompson a goalscoring opportunity. If City were struggling to get at Chelsea with 11, playing with 10 made the task impossible.

Bompastor got her tactical approach spot on at Stamford Bridge, balancing enough risk with sensible stability. But she was reliant on perfect execution of the game plan from her players. They delivered. None more so than evergreen Bronze.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Another to confess to "love defending" at the weekend was Mary Earps.

Her heroism in defending London City's goal at the Emirates earned her side a valiant point against Arsenal as they continue to hold on to third spot while also staying in touch with the top two. "This game sums up why I wanted to come back and play in the best league in the world," she told Sky Sports afterwards.

England fans will have fond memories of Earps in this vein, bent on denying Arsenal from any and every angle imagineable. Sarina Wiegman will too, and she was in the stands to witness one of the finest displays of goalkeeping from a player she once called her No 1.

"She has a very uniquely competitive mindset," Izzy Christiansen reflected from the studio in north London. "She's in her element. Some of the saves were world class." Earps made eight of them. Five from inside the box.

But the best was left until last. In the final throws of the game, as the Gunners pushed to turn another unwanted home draw into something more, the ball found Frida Maanum on the edge of the area. She had already scored the game's opener but Arsenal had been undone 98 seconds later and needed another moment of inspiration.

With almost no backlift at all, Maanum shaped a lovely strike towards the top corner and waited to see it nestle in the net. Except it never did. Earps was forced to backpedal but got enough purchase on her leap to claw the ball onto the crossbar and preserve the point London City deserved for their efforts. None more impressive than her own.

Claims of vintage Earps echoed around the Emirates. Social media buzzed with posts of 'Mary's back!' The WSL is certainly a better league with her in it.

Wiegman may no longer be able to call upon the 33-year-old's services, but Eder Maestre will be delighted he can. If London City are to turn their Champions League ambitions into reality, Earps' wealth of big-game experience and ability to handle pressure moments could prove invaluable.

#995. Jurgen Klopp rages at Gianni Infantino being ‘worse than Sepp Blatter’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Germany manager is upset at the way the sport has been governed by Infantino and compared him to his controversial predecessor Blatter

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Germany manager Jurgen Klopp has launched a stinging attack on the role of Gianni Infantino as Fifa president and called on him to resign.

A bemused Klopp has been left in despair at the way he interprets Infantino’s leadership of the sport: “I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that”.

Infantino’s position was at risk after a bold move to sell off the rights to the World Cup as part of a private investor plan, without the prior knowledge of the Fifa Council and national associations.

But Infantino has weathered the storm and now appears set to win a fourth term in the upcoming Fifa election, with Africa, Asia, Oceania and South America’s associations thought to be aligned with the current president.

Klopp would prefer to see a change at the head of the organisation though, suggesting Infantino compares unfavourably to his predecessor Blatter, who resigned in 2015 amid allegations of corruption.

In quotes reported by BBC Sport, Klopp said: “I’ve been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense.

“I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that.”

Klopp added: “Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job.”

The deadline for candidates to be submitted is November 18, with former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega having already announced his intention to be a rival to Infantino.

Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japanese Football Association is also reportedly set to mount a challenge and the Guardian reported on Monday that French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo could yet be a surprise contender.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger was touted as a potential challenger but it is understood he told European football’s governing body UEFA that he would not stand.

#992. England talking points: Tuchel learns Argentina lesson as full-backs shine

England beat Spain 3-2 in a statement performance and result in Madrid; the Three Lions ended the world champions' 43-game unbeaten run to top their Nations League group and be a seeded team for the quarter-finals in March; Sky Sports look at the main talking points from the big result...

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

After England beat Spain in their own back yard in a statement result, we look at the main talking points from a memorable moment in Madrid...

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

England's football DNA has been in focus this autumn. In Madrid, we saw the English style at its best. From the first whistle, England were boldly on the front foot, overwhelming Spain with pace, power and directness.

They snapped into tackles and gave short shrift to their opponents when they called for fouls. It was physical, it was aggressive. It was certainly not England trying to replicate the Spanish style.

The set-piece routine for the second goal was a reflection of how those phases have risen in importance in the Premier League and fittingly saw two Arsenal players combine to score it. Then, when down to 10 men, there was fight, heart and commitment to get over the line.

Roy Keane called England's performance "perfect" at half-time. The errors from Jarell Quansah, Elliot Anderson and Anthony Gordon meant it certainly couldn't be called that in the end. But England's attitude and approach outweighed their mistakes. This is football England fans will get behind.Peter Smith

Tuchel didn't want to be drawn too much on comparisons between this win and the World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina.

He signalled a few times that the main takeaways about his team should come in the first 65 minutes before the red card - and even said the dogged defensive display was more like the last 16 win over Mexico. "The Azteca reloaded," he said.

But the England manager has clearly learned his lessons from the Argentina heartbreak. This was a very different approach to hanging on.

There was no back five this time. Not for a single second, even with the man disadvantage. It was so different to the World Cup. Against Argentina, he went to a back five on 72 minutes. Against Mexico, it was Dan Burn time on 75 minutes.

But Elliot Anderson's red card prompted no panic from the England bench. Anderson's hole was replaced by Jude Bellingham, who shifted back from the No 10 role. The first sub came with 10 minutes to go. Burn was only introduced on 89 minutes, but only for another defender.

There was trust from the England manager that his team could hold off the best team in the world in a back four defensive shape. That confidence led to a composed challenge, whereas against Argentina, there wasn't that faith.

And as a result, England fans have more faith in Tuchel.Sam Blitz

'Harry Kane, he's the best in the world' sang the England supporters about their Ballon d'Or winner, goading their Spanish hosts and a certain Lamine Yamal who finished in third place for the coveted prize.

In the build-up to this game, Spain player after Spain player came out to say their team-mate should have won it instead of Kane. But England's captain showed his brilliance where it mattered - on the pitch.

He won and coolly converted the penalty for the opening goal. Nerves of steel after crucially missing from the spot against the same opponents in September. He helped orchestrate the third goal, too, which was just one example of his many connections with Jude Bellingham.

England's record scorer and record appearance-maker is at the peak of his powers right now.Peter Smith

This was the night Lewis Hall went to a whole new level.

He won praise earlier this year for the way he marshalled Lamine Yamal at St James' Park in the Champions League. But Barcelona put seven past Newcastle in the second leg of that tie, so there was no guarantee this would be a positive experience for the left-back.

Hall, however, leaves Madrid with the England left-back spot nailed down and plenty wondering why he wasn't at the World Cup.

There was brilliant defending, including a couple of tackles just before half-time where he single-handedly stopped Lamine Yamal and Mikel Merino in the England box. And even in the final seconds, he expertly won a goal-kick when Alex Baena threatened.

His appetite to take the game to Spain also impressed. He made five dribbles, epitomising England's front-foot gameplan. An all-round excellent display.Peter Smith

Imagine scoring to put England 3-0 up against Spain in Madrid and it's not your best moment of the match.

For Ben White, that standout moment came on 84 minutes. With Nico Williams bearing down on goal, White pulled off a superb sliding challenge as the last defender to prevent the one-on-one.

It was like Djed Spence against Argentina all over again, only this time England got the job done.

White has completed an incredible comeback in England colours. For so long, many thought he'd never play for his country again. Many have hounded him for coming back into the fold.

But this time the headlines are not about England fans booing him. Now it's whether he can hold down this right-back spot as his own.

Like Hall at left-back, England's right-back spot has been far from settled. White is England's sixth starting right-back in their last 11 games, dating back to the start of the World Cup knockout stages.

But this was a reminder of how good White is, why he deserves his England spot after impressing for the best club team in the country.Sam Blitz

Tuchel was keen to play down talk of James Trafford ousting Jordan Pickford as England's No 1 after the game. But the young goalkeeper showed he has the ability to shine on the biggest stage in Madrid.

His double save late in the game was a decisive moment, with his reactions to keep out the second, deflected shot razor sharp. Tuchel was equally keen to praise his distribution and composure as England built up from deep.

He may have conceded five goals in two appearances against Spain in this Nations League group phase but he comes out of this period with his reputation enhanced and as the clear challenger to Pickford.

The Everton shot-stopper has never let England down but if the changing of the guard is to come in the near future, Trafford is in pole position to step in.Peter Smith

The two-legged ties are scheduled for the March international break, with the first legs to be played between March 25 and 27 and the second legs between March 28 and 30.

#991. Nike to replace Adidas as Champions League and Uefa ball supplier from 2027

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Nike is set to replace Adidas as the official match ball provider for the Champions League and all other Uefa men’s club competitions from 2027.

The deal, which runs until 2031, was announced on Monday, bringing an end to Adidas’ long-running association with the Champions League.

Nike will provide the official match balls for the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League - marking the first time all three tournaments will have the same supplier - as well as ⁠the Super Cup, Uefa Youth League and ​Uefa ⁠Futsal Champions League.

The deal was announced by UC3, the commercial joint venture between UEFA and European Football Clubs (EFC), which launched the tender process in March, and its agency Relevent Football Partners.

The Athletic reported that the deal is worth around $45m per year.

Nike Football vice president and general manager said: “We are excited and honoured to return to the Uefa Champions ‌League, one of football's biggest stages, after more ‌than two decades, and to bring Nike match balls across Uefa’s men's club competitions.

“Football is the ⁠world's game, and the ball is at the centre of it, the one thing every player, in every competition, has in common. This is a long-term commitment for Nike.

“We will listen to the athlete's voice, push the edges of innovation, honour the prestige and tradition of these competitions, and make sure the ball represents the instinct, creativity and joy football brings ‌to billions of fans.”

Analysts had said the deal would boost Nike's ​visibility but was unlikely to address the company's underlying challenges, ‌including slowing sales and a lag ⁠in product innovation that have stymied the sportswear giant in recent ⁠years.

“In terms of getting its groove back, high-visibility corporate partnerships are not the silver bullet,” ‌Zacks Investment Research analyst ​David Bartosiak had said.

“Whether you're reinventing ‌the wheel or reinventing the ball, ​you're still not bringing any sort of meaningful innovation.”

England weren't at their best against Croatia on Thursday, but they didn't need to be. A 2-1 win at Wembley, sealed by a penalty from Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane, ensured they remain in control of their own destiny.

Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions couldn't have asked for a tougher test in their final group fixture. They face European champions and World Cup winners Spain in Madrid, less than two months after losing to them at Wembley.

Lamine Yamal, Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal scored Spain's goals in a 3-2 victory that night, with Baena on the scoresheet again as Luis de la Fuente's side beat Czech Republic 2-0 on Thursday.

A draw would be enough for Spain to finish top, but the job is effectively done for both teams already. England, three points behind heading into the final fixture, have won all four of their games against Czech Republic and Croatia – not surprising, but satisfactory.

Their last win against Spain came in the Nations League in Seville eight years ago, when Raheem Sterling, Marcus Rashford and Kane all got on the scoresheet. There's been plenty of water under the bridge since then.

Last time Spain lost a match was March 2024 and they haven't even had to settled for a draw since Cape Verde.

#989. Record-breaking Ebola outbreak: phone data reconstruct first weeks of spread

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Confirmed infections of Bundibugyo Ebola have surpassed 10,000 in the DRC since May.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock

Epidemiologists have used mobile-phone data and test records to map the early spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)1 weeks before the outbreak was declared. The authors say the study findings reveal how surveillance systems failed to detect signals of the disease early on and enabled it to spread rapidly.

It is now six months since the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus was announced. The number of confirmed infections has risen to more than 10,000 and 5,198 people have died, making this the largest Bundibugyo outbreak so far. There are no licenced vaccines or approved treatments specifically for Bundibugyo, which has complicated efforts to control it.

The DRC declared the outbreak on 15 May after laboratory tests confirmed the first case, a person from Ituri province in the country’s northeast, was infected with the Bundibugyo strain. Around the same time, suspected cases were being reported in several DRC locations, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara, Bunia and Nyankunde in Ituri, and Butembo, Katwa and Goma in the neighbouring province of North Kivu. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on 17 May, citing infections among health-care workers, the geographical spread of cases and clusters of undocumented deaths. Researchers strongly suspect that the virus had been spreading in the region months earlier.

To understand how the outbreak spread so quickly, the researchers looked at anonymized mobile-phone data to trace the movement of people between areas.

Although the first confirmed case was identified on 15 May, the study reports that the person had symptoms as early as 25 April.

The team found that people travelling out of Mongbwalu, Bunia and Rwampara between 24 April and 24 May helped to predict which health zones would report infections by 1 June. For instance, areas close to the initial centres were at greater risk of infections, the study found.

The risk of infections rose again in places 150–200 kilometres away from the initial outbreak centres because people travelled to larger towns and cities along established routes, says study co-author Pierre Akilimali, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) in Kinshasa.

The authors say the findings show that people movement was a key driver of the rapid spread in the early phases of the outbreak.

“These are very important findings which reinforce what we initially knew at the onset of the outbreak,” says Tambe Akem, an independent public-health consultant based in Yaoundé, Cameroon.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03666-z

Ebengo. D. M. et al. Science https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aej4586 (2026).

#988. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

#987. Ten-man England hold on to claim famous win over Spain

Spain vs England. UEFA Nations League Group A3.

Match report as England secure a stunning 3-2 win over Spain to end the world champions' 43-game unbeaten run and finish top of Nations League Group A3; Three Lions raced into a three-goal lead then clung on after Elliot Anderson's red card

Football Features Writer @nicholaspwright

England withstood a Spain fightback after Elliot Anderson's red card to secure a famous 3-2 victory and finish above the world champions at the top of their Nations League group.

Thomas Tuchel's side were sensational for an hour in Madrid, taking the lead when Harry Kane scored a penalty at the end of the first half and then adding quickfire goals from Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

But a one-sided game was turned on its head when Elliot Anderson was sent off for a last-man foul on Lamine Yamal following Jarell Quansah's error, allowing Mikel Oyarzabal to score from the spot.

Spain reduced the deficit to one goal when substitute Nico Williams converted Lamine Yamal's cross after Anthony Gordon had been dispossessed, but England clung on thanks to James Trafford.

The goalkeeper, selected ahead of Jordan Pickford, made a string of saves as Spain peppered the England goal, including a stunning double stop when he denied Fermin Lopez then somehow pushed Oyarzabal's follow-up around the post at full stretch.

His heroics, in addition to a vital last-man challenge by White on Williams, allowed the Three Lions to end Spain's 43-game unbeaten run with a historic victory which ensures they will be seeded in the Nations League quarter-final draw.

It appeared certain to be a more emphatic victory when White drilled the third goal through the legs of Unai Simon after Konsa had headed in Declan Rice's corner for the second. Spain had not even registered a shot on target at that point.

But Anderson's red card, after Quansah was caught on the ball by Lamine Yamal, reinvigorated Spain and meant England had to show the qualities demonstrated in their World Cup last-16 win over Mexico at the Azteca Stadium in July.

Their steel, and the contribution of their goalkeeper, got them over the line - and showed evidence of progress from their World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina, when they lost their lead late on.

"We are fully aware of the performance we put out there for 60-65 minutes. To be 3-0 up and deservedly 3-0 up.

"Of course the red card and penalty changed the momentum and the characteristic of the game. Thirty minutes against Spain, in Spain, feels like three hours.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"That is the statement and significance of this victory: that it was deserved and the result followed the performance.

"It was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit and togetherness. It was on the highest level football-wise on all aspects of the game.

"That was an excellent performance. A wonderful feeling in the dressing room. Everyone was very tired. We overcame some difficult moments.

"We're aware of what steps we took now after the World Cup. It's the best feeling."

England captain Harry Kane on Spain's pre-match World Cup trophy parade:

"If anything, that made us more hungry. It gave us the bit between the teeth to say 'okay, it's four months later but we're the team that's going to go on and be the next European and world champions.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"We still have to prove that, of course. We still have a long way to go. Nights like tonight will only help the belief in the team. It shows what we are doing. When we talk about it, it's one thing. When we show it against the best team in the world, then of course that's a rewarding factor.

"We're not a team that wants to retreat. We want to sit back and go again. Show the type of team we are when we are at our best. Full tempo, high press, winning balls back, running in behind, counter-attacking.

"We were hard to stop in abundance in the first 60 minutes. Then in the last 30 you lean on experiences in the Azteca and those types of games. I was speaking to Dec [Rice] out there saying that we have been through worse than this, and it shows.

"There were no big big chances. [James Trafford] made some amazing saves, the double saves towards the end of course, but when you can hold on to a lead against Spain with 10 men away, it shows the mental aspect."

"We knew we could beat them. We knew we were going to beat them today.

"The message from the manager after the Croatia game was so positive. The message from the boys, everyone pushing together, knowing that we're going to come here and not sit back and hit them on the counter.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"We knew from the first minute - our first 10 minutes was probably the best we've played in a 10-minute spell. Pressure, pressure, pressure, we could have had two or three.

"The red card changes the course of the game as it could have been a couple more goals if I'm being honest."

England's football DNA has been in focus this autumn. In Madrid, we saw the English style at its best. From the first whistle, England were boldly on the front foot, overwhelming Spain with pace, power and directness.

They snapped into tackles and gave short shrift to their opponents when they called for fouls. It was physical, it was aggressive. It was certainly not England trying to replicate the Spanish style.

The set-piece routine for the second goal was a reflection of how they have risen in importance in the Premier League and fittingly saw two Arsenal players combine to score it. Then, when down to 10 men, there was fight, heart and commitment.

Roy Keane called England's performance "perfect" at half-time. The errors from Quansah, Anderson and Gordon meant it certainly couldn't be called that in the end. But England's attitude and approach outweighed their mistakes.

This is football England fans will get behind.

England find out who they will face in the Nations League quarter-finals when the draw takes place on Friday November 20 at 11am.

The two-legged ties are scheduled for the March international break, with the first legs to be played between March 25 and 27 and the second legs between March 28 and 30.

#985. Why James Trafford must now be England’s No 1

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Trafford’s brilliant performance in England’s win over Spain means that he now deserves to supplant Jordan Pickford in England’s goalkeeping stakes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As auditions go, it could hardly have been better. James Trafford was given the opportunity to show that he genuinely belongs in the England No 1 conversation by facing the world champions in their own back yard and he excelled.

England outclassed Spain for an hour and then produced a backs-to-the-wall display for the final 30 minutes to cling on for a famous 3-2 triumph – their first ever away victory over a team ranked No 1 in the world and a first win over Spain in Madrid since 1987. In other words, historic, and the defining memory of the clash will be Trafford’s remarkable double save in injury time to preserve the narrow advantage.

The 24-year-old brilliantly repelled Fermin Lopez’s effort before recovering almost instantly to get across and somehow tip Aymeric Laporte’s rebound past the post. He was mobbed by teammates and while no England stop will ever have the same resonance of Gordon Banks’ almost mythical save from Pele at the 1970 World Cup, this immediately enters the tier just below.

He made six saves in total throughout the game – a number only bettered three times by England goalkeepers in the past 15 years according to WhoScored – and even in a first half where he had little shot-stopping to do, looked supremely comfortable on the ball and was accurate in his distribution. He was vital in beating the energetic Spanish press.

Leeds United paid a record £45m fee for a British goalkeeper to prise him away from Manchester City this summer and that is already looking like a snip. He has the highest save percentage in the Premier League this year (82.2 per cent according to FBRef ), while only the league’s top two sides, Arsenal and Brighton, have conceded fewer than the Whites’ eight goals. Trafford has been a key part of a Leeds defence that is suddenly one of the meanest around and has enabled Daniel Farke’s men to establish themselves in the top half of the table.

A penny for Enzo Maresca’s true thoughts. Given Gianluigi Donnarumma’s inconsistent form this season, there’s a strong argument that City jettisoned the wrong goalkeeper this summer and that the Englishman – who is not only better with the ball at his feet but also three years younger than the Italian – will prove to be the superior player. Perhaps he is already.

In his four previous England caps, starting with his debut against Uruguay at Wembley back in March, he looked at ease, only really leaving the question of whether he could perform under pressure against the very, very best in the world and his display in Madrid answered that emphatically. Tournament football is another level entirely but at this point, it would be foolish to bet against Trafford stepping up and delivering on that stage as he has done at every other.

Which is why it’s now time for him to be anointed as England’s No 1 as they build towards Euro 2028. This is not to disparage Jordan Pickford, who has performed remarkably for England and continues to be a top-level goalkeeper but the upside play at this point is Trafford. The Three Lions have consistently fallen agonisingly short of getting over the line in major tournaments and, to be clear, Pickford holds zero blame for that fact, but the pursuit of such an elusive goal requires brave decisions to improve the fine margins and officially elevating Trafford qualifies.

Thomas Tuchel has already begun the process by splitting starts equally between previously undisputed No 1 Pickford and pretender Trafford over the past two international breaks. It’s notable that the more inexperienced man has been given the two assignments against world champions Spain. He could have been in goal for the more routine clash with Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, with Pickford between the sticks in Madrid, but instead Tuchel rightly decided he would learn more by Trafford entering the Metropolitano cauldron – and his man emerged without even being singed.

The German was non-committal when asked post-match whether he now has a new first choice. “There’s no number one,” insisted Tuchel. “It’s a good double save [at the end]. That’s what we wanted. He had a brilliant match. It only works if you’re top from number one to 11.”

But the England boss will quietly be thrilled with the selection headache he now has and it does feel like a changing of the guard is slowly occurring. It may be harsh on Pickford, who has been generally underrated during his tenure as Three Lions No 1, but elite sport is a necessarily emotionless arena.

Pickford has been consistently outstanding since his international debut in a 0-0 draw against Germany at Wembley in 2017, with Opta stats claiming he has made only two errors leading to goals in 94 appearances, with 46 clean sheets and a 74 percent save ratio. He has made 33 appearances at major tournaments and been an integral part of England’s most sustained period of competitiveness (two world Cup semi-finals, two Euros finals) in their history.

Since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya (39) has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford (27) at Everton and even this year, he is in a creditable sixth spot with a 73.7 save percentage in the Premier League.

He has never made a glaring mistake that has cost England in a big game but, under the radar, he had a slightly rocky World Cup this summer. Martin Baturina’s shot slipped through his hands for Croatia’s first of two goals and in the last-32 win over DR Congo, the 32-year-old was beaten too easily at his near post by Brian Cipenga’s shot for their opening goal. He was fortunate not to be sent off against Ghana when he ill-advisedly came off his line and clattered Prince Adu outside of the box.

Television cameras also caught Pickford in an animated conversation with Tuchel after a botched clearance at one point, with the goalkeeper giving as good as he got before his manager ended the discussion by shouting “do as I told you!”

Throughout his England career, Pickford’s distribution has been decent, although sometimes patchy and Trafford presents a clear step up in that department. Purely in terms of physicality, the younger man’s 6ft 6in frame somewhat dwarfs the 6ft 1in Everton star. He has surpassed his rival in a number of ways.

Pickford should go down as one of England’s greatest goalkeepers – even if there is a somewhat surprising hesitance from many to bestow him with that honour – and he will deservedly clear 100 caps. But the time has come for James Trafford to be crowned as No 1. He’s earned it.

#983. Grand Slam of Darts: Four seeds crash out as Greaves exits despite win

Four seeds were sent crashing out of the tournament on a bumper Sunday while women's star Greaves beat Niels Zonneveld; watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports with the final taking place on Sunday November 22

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Seeds Jonny Clayton, Ross Smith, Josh Rock and Luke Woodhouse were all knocked out of the Grand Slam of Darts on Sunday, while Beau Greaves was also eliminated.

Fifth seed Clayton was demolished 5-1 in barely 10 minutes by former world champion Rob Cross, who posted an impressive 114 average and finishing stats of 83 per cent.

Clayton was the second seed to be eliminated on Sunday after 15th-seed Luke Woodhouse lost 5-1 to Krzysztof Ratajski.

In the final match of the afternoon session, eighth seed Josh Rock knew he could not afford to lose three legs to Kevin Doets, but he ultimately lost the match 5-3.

And in the evening session, sixth seed Smith beat Gabriel Clemens 5-4, but conceded too many legs and exits the tournament following Saturday's shock loss to Rusty-Jake Rodriguez.

Meanwhile, three-time Women's World Matchplay champion Greaves enjoyed a 5-3 win against Niels Zonneveld, but the scoreline was not enough to keep her in the competition.

Lisa Ashton, Cam Crabtree, Raymond Smith, Adam Sevada, Maik Kuivenhoven, Jan Schmidt, Carl Sneyd and Joe Hunt also had group-stage exits confirmed on Sunday.

Group A: Niels Zonneveld 3-5 Beau Greaves

Beau Greaves recovered from 3-1 down to beat Niels Zonneveld 5-3, but the scoreline was not good enough to see her progress from this year's 'Group of Death'.

Greaves dominated her opponent in the second half of the match, but her 5-2 defeat to Luke Littler on Saturday night sees her once again fail to get out of a group with The Nuke now the hot favourite to progress to the last 16.

Lisa Ashton will need to wait another year for her first win in the Grand Slam of Darts, as she fell to a 5-2 loss to Alan Soutar. That result means whoever wins Monday's clash between Soutar and Jermaine Wattimena will progress.

After losing his opening match to Tommy Morris on Saturday, Premier League star Josh Rock knew he needed to beat Kevin Doets and concede no more than two legs in order to stay in the tournament.

However, Doets posted a 100 average and five 180s as he stormed to a 5-3 victory to eliminate Rock and set up a Monday night showdown with Morris.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Group D: Cameron Menzies 5-4 Raymond Smith

Cameron Menzies fought back from 3-1 down to beat Raymond Smith 5-4 and set up a Monday night decider with Stephen Bunting to see who tops the group.

A spectacular 162 finish in the sixth leg levelled the scores and helped to eliminate the unfortunate Smith, who lost final-leg deciders in both of his matches at the Grand Slam.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Joe Hunt averaged more than 94 and threw a dozen 140s, but was still eliminated from the Grand Slam of Darts in a thrilling 5-4 defeat to Sebastian Bialecki on Sunday evening.

The Polish player edged a last-leg decider to pick up two points and he will now face Gerwyn Price on Monday night to decide who reaches the knockout stage.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Group F: Andrew Gilding 5-4 Charlie Manby

Andrew Gilding averaged just 81, but still found a way to eliminate Charlie Manby from the Grand Slam with a 5-4 victory.

Manby missed his first 12 darts at double in the match before recovering to establish a 3-2 lead, but his opponent won three of the final four legs, ultimately securing the win with a classy 124 checkout on bullseye. He will face Ryan Searle on Monday to decide who progresses.

Jonny Clayton won the opening leg of his must-win clash against Rob Cross, but didn't attempt another double as he was knocked out of the tournament in brutal fashion.

Cross reeled off five legs in a row, including finishes of 138 and 137 in a ruthless performance and will look to take that form into his group decider with Anton Ostlund on Monday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Niko Springer managed TWO Robin Hoods (where a dart lands in the flight of a previous dart and scores no points) but still cruised to a 5-1 win over Adam Sevada.

That means the winner of Springer's clash with Wessel Nijman on Monday night will reach the last 16.

Joe Cullen suffered a surprise defeat to Paolo Nebrida who kept his hopes of qualification alive with a 5-2 victory.

In a game of poor-quality finishing, the players missed 30 darts at a double between them in seven legs, and while Luke Humphries is now a heavy favourite to progress from Group I, all three players can still technically qualify.

Group J: Luke Woodhouse 1-5 Krzysztof Ratajski

World No 17 Luke Woodhouse became one of the biggest casualties of the tournament so far as he lost five legs in a row in a 5-1 defeat to Krzysztof Ratajski.

That makes it two defeats in two games for 'Woody', while Ratajski will take on Tom Sykes on Tuesday night to decide who makes it into the next round.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

After losing 5-1 to James Wade on Saturday, Cam Crabtree needed to avoid losing two legs against Ricky Evans on Sunday to stay in the competition.

The pair served up a quickfire contest to the Wolverhampton crowd and Crabtree missed two match darts, but was ultimately knocked out by Evans who will now face Wade to decide the group.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Group L: Jeffrey de Graaf 4-5 Henry Coates

Henry Coates took Michael van Gerwen to a last-leg decider on Saturday night and the 20-year-old was involved in another thriller on Sunday as he beat Jeffrey de Graaf 5-4.

The result means all three players could still technically qualify from the group.

Carl Sneyd's tournament was ended by an impressive display from Bradley Brooks, who threw five 180s and averaged more than 97 in a 5-3 win.

Brooks will now take on third seed Gian van Veen on Tuesday night, seeking an upset victory to make his way into the second round.

Group N: Martin Schindler 5-0 Jan Schmidt

Martin Schindler whitewashed Jan Schmidt 5-0 in the opening match of the evening session to eliminate his fellow German from the tournament.

Both players struggled on their doubles, but Schindler is the only player who hasn't lost a leg and can now focus on Tuesday's winner-takes-all clash with Chris Dobey to decide who tops the group.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Ross Smith was one of the favourites to win the Grand Slam of Darts, but exits at the group stage despite a gutsy win over Gabriel Clemens.

The European champion needed to win 5-3 or better to keep his tournament hopes alive, but a checkout ratio of less than 19 per cent proved his undoing.

Group P: Karel Sedlacek 4-5 Maik Kuivenhoven

Maik Kuivenhoven was eliminated from the tournament but still recovered from 4-1 down to beat Karel Sedlacek 5-4.

That leaves Sedlacek needing a big win over Nathan Aspinall on Tuesday night to qualify.

#981. Nathan Collins ruled out of Ireland’s crunch Nations League clash with Kosovo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Irish captain will miss the must-win contest due to injury

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Heimir Hallgrimsson has been dealt a blow with captain Nathan Collins ruled out of the Republic of Ireland’s must-win Nations League clash with Kosovo.

The centre-back has returned to Brentford and will be replaced by Jimmy Dunne in the squad for the Republic’s final meeting of Group B3, where a win would secure them second place and a promotion play-off berth.

Collins missed the last international window with a calf issue and felt discomfort in his knee late in Saturday’s 1-0 loss to group winners Austria.

“He went for a scan here and it was decided he would go back to Brentford, doing more testing on him,” Hallgrimsson explained.

“We will wait to see what their experts will say on it, but at least he is not in our squad for the game.”

The Republic boss agreed Collins’ absence will be a big miss, adding: “But we have shown now that our depth is much better and the knowledge of what we are doing is much better than it has been.”

Kosovo are in the driver’s seat, one point clear of Ireland, who are also hoping to propel themselves into pot two for the upcoming Euro 2028 draw with victory at the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday night.

They lost the reverse fixture in Pristina 1-0 but showed plenty of promise in Linz, despite the result, and Hallgrimsson is eager to replicate those efforts.

“We need to get the same mentality, the same characters on the pitch against Kosovo,” he said.

“It is going to be as tough a game as it was in Austria, so just transfer that same attitude and if we do that we will have a good by-product, which is a win.

“It is clear we need to win the game, a draw will do nothing for us and that is our mentality going into the game.”

Hallgrimsson has no other fresh injury concerns after James Abankwah got over a cramp issue.

The Icelandic boss was full of praise for Caoimhin Kelleher, who has been a standout throughout the campaign and made several critical stops on Saturday.

The Brentford goalkeeper is aware of the impact a win could have on qualifying for what would be a home European Championships in 2028 but insists the focus remains on the immediate future.

He said: “Yeah, it would obviously be hard to describe, it would be an amazing experience, to play in a major tournament at home would be special.

“But I don’t think we can think too far ahead into that. Obviously we’ve got to focus on tomorrow and trying to get a good result and we’ll look towards that then when it comes.

“But we all know the opportunity that’s there for us if we can perform, so it’ll be a great opportunity.”

#978. Is McIlroy Europe's greatest golfer ever?

Rory McIlroy shares the record with Colin Montgomerie on eight Race to Dubai titles but faces a tougher challenge for a ninth in 2027, with Tyrrell Hatton and Jon Rahm set to return full-time to the DP World Tour; Paul McGinley says McIlroy remains "very important" to the European Tour

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rory McIlroy's quest to become the greatest European player in golfing history continued as he topped the DP World Tour's season-long Order of Merit for a record-equalling eighth time.

McIlroy has emulated Colin Montgomerie and will look to usurp the Scot with a ninth triumph in 2027 - although is aware that will be quite the feat with LIV Golf alumni Tyrrell Hatton and Jon Rahm set to make full-time returns to the European-based circuit.

The position of the continent's golfing GOAT is obviously a subjective one, but McIlroy's numbers mean he definitely deserves to be in that conversation.

No European has spent as many weeks at world No 1 as his 122. Only one European - Harry Vardon, whom the DP World Tour Order of Merit silverware is named after - has won more men's majors, with Vardon picking up seven to McIlroy's six (and possibly counting).

Should the Northern Irishman claim a ninth Harry Vardon Trophy next year - he has already publicly said he is targeting double figures in time - and perhaps also increase his tally of major titles, he may be considered Europe's unequivocal kingpin.

Speaking after a second-placed finish to Hatton at the DP World Tour Championship, McIlroy said: "Some things mean more to me than other things.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I feel a theme of my career over the last few years is trying to get to a point where other people may consider me as the best European that's ever played.

"I'm a proud European. That's something that I would be very proud to achieve. Getting to eight Order of Merits and matching Monty is probably a step to doing that.

"Next year will be tough because you've got the likes of Jon [Rahm] and Tyrrell [Hatton] and some of these guys coming back playing a full-time DP World Tour schedule, [whereas] I'll be bouncing around a little bit on both the DP World Tour and the PGA Tour.

"It's certainly a big incentive [to win six Race to Dubai titles in succession]. Monty (Montgomerie) won seven in a row. It will be incredibly competitive, a little more difficult.

"I'll just have to go out there and play well and accumulate points early. If I have to beef up my schedule at the end of next year to compete with them, if I'm in with a close enough chance of doing it, I'll do that."

Rahm and Hatton are currently unable to play on the PGA Tour following their previous switches to LIV Golf, which recently announced its intention to wind down after failing to secure funding moving forward.

Under PGA Tour rules, golfers are ineligible for 12 months from their previous LIV start.

Sky Sports pundit and Ryder Cup-winning captain Paul McGinley said of McIlroy: "To be the best European of all time, you have got to win more Order of Merits, be supportive of the DP World Tour and obviously there are major championships as well.

"Those three things really push him. If you look at all the things that he does in golf, those three things are kind of what motivates him the most.

"Is the world ranking No 1 position really that important to him? I don't think so.

"It's going to be difficult next year to overtake the likes of Rahm, who will play double the tournaments that will count for Race to Dubai points than Rory. That doesn't mean he can't do it.

"I think Rory is a very important guy for the tour in a lot of areas. He's really important for his negotiations with the PGA Tour, because of his loyalty over here. The PGA Tour want a big piece of him too, but his loyalty is very much over here.

"I think he's a big ally for Guy Kinnings [DP World Tour CEO], when it comes to these negotiations that are going on.

"Let's not discount the role that he's playing for the DP World Tour going forward."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

McIlroy says his immediate target is victory at the Australian Open next month, a tournament he previously won in 2013.

He added, of an event live on Sky Sports from December 3: "That's really the next goal, get that next win. I've played a lot of good golf this year. I've only won once [at The Masters] but it was a big one.

"It would be nice to cap the year off with a victory."

The forward England star will be in attendance at the London Playing Fields Foundation’s prestigious ‘Made in London Award’ at its Gala Dinner at The Savoy on November 19

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former England and Chelsea star Joe Cole has highlighted the vital importance of protecting grassroots pitches across the capital, warning "you can’t produce any footballers without football pitches."

The 45-year-old enjoyed an illustrious playing career, which included three Premier League titles at Stamford Bridge and 56 caps for the Three Lions, and London’s local playing fields played a pivotal role in shaping his journey to the top.

Established in 1890, the charity works to safeguard the capital’s green spaces, inspiring future generations to follow in the footsteps of sporting greats. Speaking exclusively to FourFourTwo, Cole admitted the nomination means a great deal to him.

"London and football are two of the things most dearest to my heart," Cole said. "I’m a London kid. I was born in Camden Town, and obviously football is my passion, so the two things together make perfect sense, and they do a great job there.

"We need to protect the green space, not just for football, but for every sport, for kids to play, particularly in London. We have a rich history of producing footballers. You can’t produce any footballers without football pitches – whether that be five-a-side, seven-a-side, 11-a-side, cricket pitches, anything for young people to go out and be active. It’s about keeping them off the developers and making sure there’s room for kids to play."

Renowned throughout his career for his street-footballer flair and close control, Cole honed his trademark skills growing up in north London during the 1980s, making the most of whatever space was available.

"I lived in a ground-floor flat with a tiny garden, so London was my back garden," Cole recalled. "There were no boundaries. There was a bit of grass right outside my house, a wall, and over the back end there was a little concrete seven-a-side pitch.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"You had to be imaginative. I used to walk to Market Road, which was one of the first AstroTurf pitches in the country. London is just a city riddled with little areas to play. I love London, I really do, and I can’t ever see myself living far from it."To learn more about the London Playing Fields Foundation visit lpff.org.uk

England's next generation came of age at the Metropolitano on Sunday night

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Succession planning is one of international football’s trickiest arts, especially when replacing a goalkeeper who has laid claim to the No. 1 shirt for nearly a decade, or trying to fix a left-back spot that has become something of a revolving door.

For Thomas Tuchel, though, the answers to two of England’s biggest long-term headaches have been forged at Elland Road and St James’ Park.

On a thrilling Sunday night in Madrid, as 10-man England stunned reigning world champions Spain 3-2 to snap La Roja’s 43-match unbeaten run, Leeds United’s James Trafford and Newcastle’s Lewis Hall announced themselves as the next generation of Three Lions stalwarts.

For almost 10 years, Jordan Pickford’s status as England’s undisputed No. 1 has been largely uninterrupted, stretching from the 2018 World Cup to last summer’s semi-final run in North America. It left little room for an understudy to build experience or a case for selection.

Moving on from a 94-cap mainstay is never straightforward, which is why Trafford’s decision to swap Manchester City’s bench for regular Premier League football at Leeds in August has proven so vital for Tuchel. Playing week-in, week-out has helped the 24-year-old develop into a ready-made alternative capable of taking the gloves whenever Pickford eventually hangs his up.

Handed a rare start at the Metropolitano and given the chance to test his temperament and big-game mentality against elite opposition, Trafford watched as goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White fired England into a 3-0 lead.

But when Elliot Anderson saw red in the 62nd minute, Leeds’ No.1 was faced with a relentless Spanish siege. Spain racked up 23 shots, seven on target and 2.73 Expected Goals (xG), yet Trafford refused to buckle.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Leeds stopper made five crucial saves - repelling Fermin Lopez from close range, recovering well to deny Lamine Yamal and Marc Cucurella, and producing an outstanding stoppage-time double save to thwart Yamal and Aymeric Laporte - all the while impressing Tuchel with his composure during build-up.

At left-back, Tuchel’s gratitude to Newcastle should be equally clear. Since Euro 2024, England have cycled through 10 different players in the role, experimenting with the likes of Nico O’Reilly and Myles Lewis-Skelly, right-footed deputies such as Djed Spence, and stopgaps. This is largely because nobody had convincingly locked down the position consistently at club level.

Many felt Hall was unfairly overlooked when Tuchel left him out of the 2026 World Cup squad, a tournament in which England’s left flank seemed to lack balance. But the 22-year-old’s emergence as an indispensable starter for Newcastle, particularly this season, has finally given Tuchel a specialist he can rely on.

Against one of the most dangerous wingers on the planet, Lamine Yamal, Hall was excellent. Defensively, he registered five clearances and two vital first-half interventions inside his own box to snuff out Yamal and Mikel Merino, before drawing two late fouls to relieve pressure in the dying seconds.

In possession, he was just as accomplished, completing five dribbles in the first half alone - more than Spain’s entire 10 outfield players combined. He found a teammate with 30 of his 34 passes (88 per cent accuracy), providing natural left-footed width that facilitated Anthony Gordon's strong performance, too.

Pickford’s experience ensures he won't be surrendering his place without a fight, and Tuchel insisted afterwards that no permanent changing of the guard has taken place. International bosses are ultimately reliant on club environments to forge their stars, so by entrusting Trafford and Hall with pivotal Premier League roles, Leeds and Newcastle are doing the heavy lifting for future tournaments.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#975. How Andy Robertson defied the odds to become Scotland’s greatest captain

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

A humble Robertson insists he is not on the level of Sir Kenny Dalglish, despite drawing level with the legendary forward on 102 caps, but Jamie Braidwood outlines how the captain carved out a unique legacy through work-ethic and commitment

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It was a burst from the left wing that would be seen time and time again. Andy Robertson’s first goal for Scotland came on just his fourth appearance for his country, at 20 years old and only a few months after completing a £2.85m move from Dundee United to Hull City. The wider importance of the goal was ultimately forgotten, a late consolation against England in a 3-1 defeat at Celtic Park. But for Robertson, with his wide-eyed excitement and the determination to carry his run forward, it was the moment that set the tone for what was to follow.

Twelve years later, Robertson has joined the great Sir Kenny Dalglish on 102 caps after featuring in Scotland’s 2-1 victory against North Macedonia at Hampden, and another appearance tonight against Switzerland will take him clear. Passing his hero and legend for both his childhood club, Celtic, and adopted one, Liverpool, will make the Tottenham defender Scotland men’s record appearance holder on 103. It is only in keeping with Robertson’s humility that he is the first to insist Dalglish remains Scotland’s greatest player; it is only in keeping with Dalglish’s typical wry humour that he reminds Robertson that his own tally of international appearances would be much higher had competitions like the Nations League been around in his day.

“It’s not really about me,” Robertson said ahead of taking the record. "It’s about him [Dalglish] in my opinion. For how long the record stood, for what he achieved in his career, for the person he is.”

Hampden celebrated Robertson, too. What is not up for debate is the scale of achievement and the remarkable nature of his journey. His story is well known yet will be retold many times this week: how a boy released by Celtic for being too small and who worked in the Hampden ticket office while playing part-time with Queen’s Park would become one of the world’s best left-backs and a Champions League and Premier League winner.

With Scotland, part of Robertson’s legacy is formed by qualifying for three major tournaments in five years, when the Tartan Army had not previously been on the big stage since 1998. Robertson was the leader on each campaign under Steve Clarke, from the penalties against Serbia to reach Euro 2020 to beating Spain and Norway to deservedly make Euro 2024. Then, in the delirium that was Scotland’s win over Denmark to qualify for the World Cup, it was Robertson who provided another moment of inspiration when he poignantly remembered his late friend Diogo Jota and the promise they had made to each other while watching the 2022 World Cup four years before.

Robertson has led his nation with dignity and class and if insists that Dalglish remains the King, the counter is to suggest that he stands, by some way, as Scotland’s greatest captain. He has worn the armband 80 times, with an 81st cap as skipper to come in St Gallen, putting him well clear of George Young, on 48, and Billie Bremner, on 39. Robertson took on the armband just four years after his senior debut, at the age of 24. Should he continue through to Euro 2028 and Scotland, as co-hosts, ensure their place, he may lead the Tartan Army at a fourth major tournament and mark a 10-year stint as captain. The history of the Scotland men’s national team is around 150 years old, yet he would hold another record.

Euro 2028 could be important in another respect. For although Scotland have enjoyed a golden period in terms of qualifying for major tournaments, they have underperformed in all of them and have yet to escape the group stage. The missing piece for this generation of players, which they could hold above those of the past, remains out of reach. For Robertson, he will not need reminding that Clarke’s considerable achievements as head coach come with the reality that Scotland failed to perform on the big stage, with the 1-0 win over Haiti in Boston in June their only victory in nine attempts at major tournaments. Now under a fourth head coach with Scotland, in Sebastien Pocognoli, there is still time to amend that, with a chance to still secure promotion to League A, should they beat the Swiss and receive a favour from North Macedonia.

It has not helped Robertson that during his time as Scotland captain two of the other home nations have been led by talismanic captains in Harry Kane and Gareth Bale, players who brought attacking inspiration and who could change a game in the flick of a switch. Robertson’s rise and formidable peak at Liverpool came when he was part of a machine, where the driving runs of the flying left-back fitted in with the movement of the front three and the organisation of the midfield. At Scotland, Robertson has provided plenty of assists and thrust, but, unlike his old team-mate Trent Alexander-Arnold, he is not the sort to orchestrate from full-back.

Robertson has, however, worked to squeeze everything he could possibly get from his career. Perhaps it was overcoming rejection that made him take nothing for granted, but Robertson has made history by turning the ordinary into extraordinary: by showing up camp after camp, for never letting his country down. There is the work-ethic, the commitment, the desire to push for every cap as if it is his last. There are the personal touches, too, forming a spirit and a togetherness that took a Scotland squad further than they had done in a generation. But above all, Robertson continued to play the game in the way he always vowed to: as if he was a fan who had just come down from the stands. And in his relentless pursuit, he has made a nation proud along the way.

#974. Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay

The England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London

Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.

Manchester United were decided on a January move - until they brought in their new manager

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United could be about to renege on a transfer that looked to be a dead cert.

The Red Devils have just appointed Mauricio Pochettino, with the United States manager arriving at Old Trafford after a decade of speculation linking him with the hot seat.

That means that plenty of plans are changing behind the scenes, and now reports suggest that a deal that looked to be definitely happening is now under threat.

Manchester United have suffered a terrible start to the season under Michael Carrick, winning just three fixtures so far, with disharmony setting in at Carrington.

Captain Bruno Fernandes criticised the team's tactics in the defeat away at Como, while World Cup winner Lisandro Martinez has been vocal about the club's recruitment strategy over the summer.

A new report from Sport Witness says that Martinez is linked with a move to Barcelona, but that Pochettino's arrival may “ruin” that particular deal.

The Argentine looked to have one foot out the door after a disastrous performance away to Chelsea earlier this season, with Atletico Madrid and Barcelona linked with a move.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

It has been claimed that personal terms between Atleti and Martinez are not a problem, too.

With Martinez's contract at United expiring at the end of the season – with the option for an extra year – a January sale looked all but certain, but with Pochettino arriving at the club, that could well be halted, as the Argentine looks to reintegrate his compatriot into a defence that has shown very little consistency this term.

Pochettino has operated with a back three and back four over the years, with Martinez an option to play on the left side of a centre-back pairing or trio.

The former Ajax man is also capable of playing in a left-back role, with Luke Shaw recently injured.

Martinez is worth €45m, according to Transfermarkt. United take on Liverpool when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#972. HENRY WINTER: Jordan Pickford has seen off five England challengers but hasn't faced a threat quite like James Trafford
